newsitem.title: singapore: Asia-Europe talks said positive, avoiding issues.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Europe talks said positive, avoiding issues.

text.p: Foreign ministers from 25 countries met on Saturday to chart the future of ties between Europe and Asia, avoiding sensitive issues, delegates said.

"We're not talking about special issues but rather about how to proceed in ASEM (Asia-Europe Meeting) to talk about international and regional issues to avoid duplication of other forums," Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters

The Asia-Europe meeting followed a conference between the European Union (EU) and the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) earlier this week that was marked by frank exchanges over human rights, especially on Burma.
Burma is due to join ASEAN -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- possibly as early as this year.
Japan, China and South Korea joined the ASEAN countries on the Asian side for the ASEM talks with the 15-member European Union to prepare for a second Asia-Europe summit due in London next April.
Burma, whose top officials are banned from Europe, could be a problem unless a solution is found before the London summit.
Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn said ASEAN wanted Europe to coax Burma's pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi into dropping her call for international sanctions against Rangoon.
He told reporters that the EU wanted Southeast Asia to put pressure on Burma's military rulers to improve their human rights record.
"We would like the West to do the same thing and talk to Aung San Suu Kyi to turn down her decision and give her hand to the other side," he said.
Suu Kyi has called repeatedly for sanctions against Burma's State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), which seized power in 1988 and ignored the results of subsequent elections her party won.
Delegates said Burma was not specifically discussed on Saturday and the ASEM talks focused more on how to talk about the issues than the issues themselves.
"The situation is very positive," said Dutch official Roland van den Berg.
"No specific problems were discussed. It was more at this stage to identify the scope of the political dialogue and I think it was very clear there was a very open concept," he said.

Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar told delegates at a welcoming dinner on Friday that ASEM completed the third leg of a global strategic triangle, after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) grouping and the close links between North America and Europe.
"The weak link in this triangular relationship was between Asia and Europe," Jayakumar said.
"ASEM must strengthen the political dialogue between the two regions on the basis of equality and mutual respect," he said.
Asian delegates complained that the Europeans were more interested in talking about political issues than trade liberalisation, which is the Asian priority.
European delegates said a political dimension was important to the talks. "The Asians want to have the economic cooperation and the technology transfer without all the lectures," one said.
The delegates were expected to talk about possibly expanding ASEM to include other Asian and European countries such as Australia, India or Russia.
The meeting was to conclude on Saturday with the opening of an Asia-Europe Foundation office in Singapore that is aimed at fostering closer cultural and educational ties.
